title: Judith Butler
summary: Judith Butler (born 1956) is an American philosopher, one of the key figures of poststructuralism, known for the theory of gender performativity. After 2001, vulnerability, grief and nonviolence move to the centre of Butler's thinking: what it means to live while depending on one another, and whose lives society recognizes as worthy of being mourned.
onEmotions: Butler thinks about feelings through relationships: from the very beginning we depend on others — on their care, their gaze, their language — and so strong feelings lay bare what we are made of. Grief, passion and rage take us "beside ourselves": in these states it becomes clear that the "I" is not an autonomous fortress but a knot of ties. Butler calls this openness to injury, shared by all living beings, precariousness, and its unequal distribution in society precarity. Another important idea is "frames": society determines in advance whose losses are noticed and whose grief is recognized — that is, which lives are "grievable." For Butler, vulnerability is not a weakness to be hidden but the ground of ethics and solidarity.

anxiety.text: Picture a body with no armour: open to the air, to touch, to other people's decisions. This is how Butler sees each of us — and would probably read your anxiety as a sensitive knowledge of that openness: there really is much in life you cannot fully protect yourself from. In Precarious Life, Butler writes that vulnerability is a condition shared by all living beings: the body is open to the world, depends on others, can be injured. Butler criticizes the fantasy of total invulnerability: the attempt to rule out risk once and for all often leads only to more tension and to closing ourselves off from others. Your anxiety is not a mistake but a sense of this openness. You don't have to defeat it; you can share it, acknowledging that others are vulnerable too — and that this is exactly why we need one another.
anxiety.practice: Look at your hands: other hands once held you just like this — fed you, led you, lifted you. Rest one palm on the other and stay for a minute with the thought that you have been in someone's hands from the very start, and right now you are holding yourself.

fear.text: In the autumn of 2001, with smoke still hanging over New York, Butler asked a question many found uncomfortable: what will a society do with its fear? Your fear is a legitimate response to the fact that you can be hurt; the question is where it will lead. It can make us build walls, divide people into "us" and "them," and seek safety by making others the vulnerable ones. Butler proposes another path: to acknowledge that precariousness is shared by all, even though it is distributed unequally (this unequal distribution is what Butler calls precarity). For you, this may mean that fear doesn't have to separate you from people. It can instead become a point of understanding: others get scared too, and all of us can be hurt. Fear recognized as shared isolates less and connects more — and becomes easier to carry.
fear.practice: Ask someone close today: "What are you afraid of right now?" — and tell them about your own fear. Notice how a shared fear sounds different from a solitary one.

sadness.text: Some funerals never take place — and Butler thinks their trace stays in us as sadness. If your sadness comes with no obvious cause, it may come from there: quiet, persistent, as if about something long ago. In The Psychic Life of Power, continuing Freud's thinking on melancholia, Judith Butler writes about losses that could not be openly acknowledged and mourned: attachments that those around us didn't consider "acceptable," possibilities we had to give up in order to meet expectations. Such unlived losses, for Butler, don't disappear — they settle inside as a quiet sadness. Your sadness may hold the memory of something you lost but were never able to name. There is a kind of faithfulness in it. Sometimes it helps simply to allow the thought: perhaps I am sad about something I was once not allowed to mourn.
sadness.practice: Hold a small farewell: switch off the light for a minute and quietly name something you once had to leave without saying goodbye. Then switch the light back on.

grief.text: "Let's face it. We're undone by each other," Butler writes in an essay on mourning, and there is no comforting untruth in that line. If you are grieving now, you know this from the inside: someone is gone, and something in you has come undone with them. In Precarious Life, Butler writes that in losing another, we realize they were part of us, that our "I" is woven out of ties. That is why grief knocks us off course: what disappears is not only the person but also part of who you were with them. Butler doesn't call for "getting over" grief and returning to how things were. Mourning, for Butler, is agreeing to undergo a change whose outcome cannot be known in advance. Another important idea is "grievability": the right of every life and every loss to be mourned. Your grief deserves recognition, however others may judge it.
grief.practice: Say the name of the one you lost out loud — slowly, as if entering it into the common register of those who are mourned. Stay for a minute in the silence after the name.

quote.text: Perhaps mourning has to do with agreeing to undergo a transformation (perhaps one should say submitting to a transformation) the full result of which one cannot know in advance.
quote.author: Judith Butler

loneliness.text: We are called by name before we have decided who we are — Butler calls this address. Loneliness is the silence where that call used to be. For Judith Butler, a person is not a separate fortress from the start: we come into the world completely dependent on others — on their care, voice, gaze — and our "I" takes shape out of these ties. That is why loneliness hurts so much: it feels not like a lack of something extra but like a wound in the very foundation. Butler calls this original embeddedness in relationships relationality: we exist only in our ties with others. Loneliness is not proof that you are unneeded but a sign that you are made for connection. It speaks the language of need, and needing others is, for Butler, not a weakness but a shared condition of human life, one that unites us rather than divides us.
loneliness.practice: Call someone and begin with their name: "Sam, I just wanted to hear your voice." Sometimes it is enough to do the calling yourself to be back inside a circle of voices.

anger.text: Nonviolence, for Butler, is not for the meek: it is a practice for people who are truly angry. Your anger, especially when it answers injustice, is for Butler a force, not a vice, and no one asks you to suppress rage. On the contrary, Butler acknowledges that aggression is part of human life and asks: what are we to do with it? The answer is nonviolence — understood not as passivity or "good behaviour" but as an active, sometimes very intense practice: holding your rage in a form that doesn't destroy your ties with others and with yourself. Butler starts from the premise that we are all interdependent: by harming another, we also undermine our own world. Your anger can be a force — not the kind that smashes, but the kind that insists, refuses to be silent, and demands justice.
anger.practice: Clench your fists as hard as you can for a count of five — then slowly open your palms. That is Butler's nonviolence in miniature: the force remains but changes form. Then say aloud one sentence you want to be heard.

shame.text: "It's a girl!" says the doctor, and for Butler this sentence begins a long performance of a norm that later looks like nature. Shame burns exactly where the performance seems to have failed: as if you were not the person you "should" be. Judith Butler shows that many such "shoulds" are not nature but norms that are repeated so often that they start to seem natural. Butler calls this idea performativity: gender, for example, is not an inner essence but something we constantly perform, in response to expectations. Shame often arises where we don't fit such norms. But if norms are created by repetition, they are not final — they can be repeated differently. Your shame speaks not of your being "wrong" but of a collision with a frame that is too narrow. You can ask yourself: whose norm is this, and does it have to be mine?
shame.practice: Say the norm that makes you ashamed in an exaggerated, theatrical voice, like an actor in a parody: "A real person always…" Butler shows that exaggeration exposes how a norm is made — listen to how it sounds from outside.

guilt.text: Butler's first ethics lessons came as a punishment: for talking too much in synagogue school, the teenager was sent to private tutorials with the rabbi. Perhaps that is where Butler's interest in answering for oneself began — and in guilt, which torments you because you care. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Judith Butler reflects on how we answer for our actions. Butler notes that we can never fully explain ourselves: our "I" has been shaped by relationships and a history we didn't choose and don't fully understand. Butler calls the demand — made of oneself or of another — for absolute transparency and flawless consistency "ethical violence." This doesn't remove responsibility, but it changes its tone: you can answer for an act while acknowledging your own limits. Then guilt becomes not endless self-accusation but a turning toward the other — a readiness to say "I'm sorry" and to hear what mattered to them.
guilt.practice: Write an account of what happened in three sentences and leave the fourth line blank — for what you don't yet understand about yourself. The blank line is part of an honest account too.

envy.text: Butler's first book is about Hegel and his scene of two consciousnesses, each hungry to be recognized by the other. Butler writes almost nothing directly about envy, but it is easy to recognize in that scene — and the unpleasant sting you feel is very human. Butler adds that we don't set the conditions of recognition: society decides in advance which lives, achievements and bodies "count." Extending Butler's thought, envy is often not about the thing itself but about recognition: the other person seems to have received the affirmation you are lacking. This helps you treat envy more gently: behind it is a normal need to be seen. And you can ask yourself who already truly sees you, and how.
envy.practice: Make a frame with your fingers and look through it at the room or the street: whatever is inside is "recognized," the rest is off-screen. Then point the frame at something in your life that no one praises but that holds you up.

emptiness.text: Accepting the Adorno Prize, Butler repeated his question: can one lead a good life in a bad life? Emptiness and apathy sometimes sound like a quiet "no" — and they are heavy partly because they are so hard to explain. In Undoing Gender, Judith Butler asks: what makes a life livable? Butler's answer is that it is not only a matter of willpower. A person needs recognition, support, connections and material conditions; without them life wears thin, even if everything looks fine from the outside. In later work, Butler stresses that no body can sustain itself alone — we all rely on others and on the world around us. Emptiness can be a sign that your supports have grown few, not that you have "forgotten how to feel." This shifts the question: not "what's wrong with me?" but "what am I missing right now in order to live more fully?"
emptiness.practice: Do one thing that supports your body the way infrastructure does: pour some water, open a window, adjust the light. Butler reminds us that life rests on such supports — notice whether it has become a little easier.

confusion.text: Butler recalls a rule from childhood: you must never "make trouble," or you will end up in trouble yourself. Confusion is a kind of trouble like that — familiar answers stop working, and that can be frightening. Yet Butler opens Gender Trouble with the conclusion that trouble and turmoil are not necessarily bad. They arise when stable categories — who I am, how to live "properly" — begin to waver. For Butler, such moments open up a possibility: what seemed natural turns out to have been made, and so it can be otherwise. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler also shows that a person is never fully transparent to themselves. Confusion is not a failure but an honest encounter with the fact that you are larger than any ready-made definition. Within it, you don't have to hurry toward answers.
confusion.practice: Imagine your "I" not as a statue but as a performance that has been running for years. Which scene in it could now be played without a script? Stay with the question for a minute without answering.

quote.text: Perhaps trouble need not carry such a negative valence. […] trouble is inevitable and the task, how best to make it, what best way to be in it.
quote.author: Judith Butler

fatigue.text: In 2011 people were sleeping in squares from Cairo to New York, and Butler noticed the essential thing: to protest, bodies need food, sleep, blankets, toilets. Even resistance rests on care. Your tiredness may be saying the same: somewhere, the supports have grown too few. In Notes Toward a Performative Theory of Assembly, Judith Butler writes that a body never holds itself up on its own — it needs food, rest, shelter, care, other people, working systems of support. When supports are few and demands keep growing, strength inevitably runs out. Butler distinguishes between the vulnerability we all share and precarity — the unequal distribution of these supports in society. Your tiredness is not only a personal story. Perhaps you are expected to hold on alone where any human being needs support. Acknowledging this dependence is not humiliating but freeing: needing rest and help is a normal human condition.
fatigue.practice: Lie down or sit so that something holds you entirely: the floor, the sofa, the back of a chair. For two minutes do nothing — just give your weight to whatever is holding you.

boredom.text: Butler reads the drag show as a lesson: the same performance, repeated a little differently, suddenly reveals that everything could be otherwise. Butler doesn't discuss boredom directly — days that all look alike, nothing catching your interest — but the theory of repetition explains a lot about it. For Butler, our life is largely made up of repetitions — gestures, roles, habitual ways of being ourselves. These repetitions sustain norms, but freedom is hidden in them too: no repetition is ever an exact copy, and in the gaps between them the possibility of doing things differently appears. Boredom may be the feeling of a repetition that has become mechanical. But it is also a hint: since your life is made of repetitions, each one holds a small chance of a shift. You don't have to change everything — you can perform something familiar a little differently and see what changes.
boredom.practice: Walk a familiar route — to the shop, around the flat, around the block — in reverse or at a different pace. For Butler, this is repetition with a shift. Notice one thing you haven't seen before.

joy.text: At a demonstration, in a choir, on a dance floor, a person suddenly forgets where they end and the crowd begins — Butler calls this being "beside oneself," in Greek ek-stasis. Butler finds this state in grief and passion, and your joy — wonderful, needing no justification — knows it from the inside. Joy, too, takes us beyond our own boundaries: we dissolve into music, into a conversation, into a shared movement. In later work, Butler also reflects on the power of people gathered together — on how, alongside others, something arises that no one has alone. Your joy is not only a personal pleasure but also a sign of connection: for a moment you stopped being a separate "I" and became part of something larger. You can simply accept this with gratitude.
joy.practice: Put on a song that makes you glad and let your body move to it for at least a minute — no mirror, no judgment. Notice the moment you become a little "beside yourself."

love.text: For Butler, to love is to let yourself be rearranged: another person enters you and moves something inside. If you love right now, you feel both the strength and the risk of that openness. For Judith Butler, this is not a flaw but the very essence of human relationships. In Precarious Life and Undoing Gender, Butler writes that we don't simply "have" ties with others — we are made by them, and in love, as in grief, this becomes obvious: another person is able to change us, to knock us out of our habits, to make us different. Butler doesn't see this as a threat that must be controlled — rather, as the truth about how we are made. Tenderness doesn't make you weak; it shows that your boundaries are alive and permeable. Accepting love means agreeing that the other "undoes" you a little, and not being afraid of it.
love.practice: Say one sentence to this person — aloud, or silently while looking at their photo: "Being with you, I've become a little different: …" Finish it with one concrete change.

quote.text: Let's face it. We're undone by each other. And if we're not, we're missing something.
quote.author: Judith Butler

gratitude.text: Your morning coffee passes through dozens of hands — pickers, drivers, sellers — and Butler asks us not to forget that invisible chain. In gratitude the chain becomes visible for a second: we don't manage alone. For Judith Butler, this is not a passing observation but the foundation of ethics: each of us lives from birth thanks to the care of others, and this interdependence doesn't end in adulthood. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler stresses that lives are bound up with one another: we breathe the same air, rely on shared homes and roads, on the labour of countless strangers. Gratitude is the moment when we acknowledge our dependence without shame. It doesn't make us debtors; it shows that we are part of a web, and brings us back to the thought that every life in this web is valuable.
gratitude.practice: Pick up any object near you — a cup, a pen, a piece of bread — and trace its path to you in your mind: who grew it, made it, brought it. Silently nod to each of them.

hope.text: Critics have often called Butler's ideas unrealistic, and Butler replies that without imagining a better world it is impossible either to live or to act. Your hope may also seem naive against the backdrop of hard news — but it is of the same stubborn kind. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler invites us to imagine a world where all lives are equally "grievable," that is, equally recognized as valuable. Butler understands that this sounds unrealistic, and deliberately defends such imagining against the charge of naivety: what is called "realism" often merely entrenches existing injustice. Hope is not a denial of reality but a refusal to treat it as final. Your hope doesn't have to be certainty. It is enough that you allow for the possibility that the world — and your life — could be arranged differently.
hope.practice: Close your eyes and picture one street in a tomorrow where every life is cherished: who is walking along it, what can be heard from the windows? Stay there for a minute without checking it for "realism."

nostalgia.text: Some smells suddenly make you seven again: your mother's soup, a stairwell, floor polish at school. Butler explains why they are so strong: in The Psychic Life of Power, a child becomes attached to those it depends on before it can choose anything, and out of these "passionate attachments" its "I" takes shape. Nostalgia, full of tenderness, is their echo: to the people, places and voices that once made us who we are. Butler shows that these ties can be complicated — love and dependence are mixed in them. That is why nostalgia can be both bright and painful. It doesn't need to be taken apart completely. You can simply acknowledge: this is where I come from, and it still lives in me.
nostalgia.practice: Find something at home that smells or sounds "like back then" — a tea, a soap, an old song — and for a minute simply breathe it in or listen. Say to yourself: "This is where I come from."

craving.text: Butler asks an awkward question: why do we cling even to what subordinates us? A sharp "I want it right now" knows that question from the inside — a craving can feel like a force impossible to resist, and there is nothing to be ashamed of here. Butler's answer, in The Psychic Life of Power, is "passionate attachment": through such a bond a person once found a footing and a way to exist. A craving is not simply weakness of will but an attachment in which an old need is hidden: for comfort, for relief, for a minute of not feeling vulnerable. Butler reminds us that vulnerability is a shared human condition, not a personal flaw. If you hear this need behind the craving, it becomes easier to wait out the wave with understanding for yourself: it rises, peaks and subsides.
craving.practice: When the wave rises, put a hand on your belly and take ten slow breaths out, counting them. On each exhale, silently say "footing" — let your breath be the footing for these minutes.

addiction.text: Every morning we "perform" ourselves anew: the same gesture, the same phrase, the same route. Butler calls this performativity — it is how gender, habits and ways of living take shape. When your life has long been organized around one thing, getting out of that circle seems almost impossible, and that is not a moral failure. Addiction also rests on repetition, which over time starts to feel like the very essence of a person: "this is who I am." But Butler's thought has a hopeful side: if something is created by repetition, it can be repeated differently — not in one leap, but through small shifts. Besides, for Butler no one lives alone: we depend on one another, and accepting support is not weakness but an ordinary human condition.
addiction.practice: Choose one person or a mutual-help group and set up a short conversation — a call, a meeting, a message saying "can we talk?" For Butler, no one steps out of a repetition alone.

hangover.text: Butler has a book whose title sounds especially pointed on a morning after: Giving an Account of Oneself. Your body hurts, memory serves up fragments of last night, anxiety and shame wash over you — and no full account comes together. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler shows that none of us can give a full account of ourselves: part of our life always remains opaque even to us. Usually this "opacity" seems like a reason for shame, but Butler draws a different conclusion: since we are not fully transparent to ourselves, ethics calls for leniency — toward others and toward ourselves. Gaps in memory and awkward recollections are not a final verdict on you. You can acknowledge that something went wrong yesterday without demanding flawless self-knowledge of yourself. Right now the most important thing is to take care of your body; sorting things out can come later.
hangover.practice: Drink a glass of water slowly, in small sips, and with each sip let go of one attempt to reconstruct last night. The account can wait — right now it's the body's turn.

euphoria.text: Ek-stasis, "standing outside oneself": Butler restores this literal meaning to the word "ecstasy" and uses it for every strong feeling — we are taken beyond our own limits. Euphoria, when everything seems possible, is exactly such a state, vivid and real. For Butler, this is not an anomaly but a laying bare of how we are made: our "I" is open to the world and to others and is never locked inside. Euphoria can be understood as a moment when this openness is felt especially keenly and joyfully. It doesn't need an explanation, and you don't need to look for a catch. You can simply notice what and whom you feel connected to in this moment — these connections, unlike the burst itself, can last a long time.
euphoria.practice: Call someone, or tell whoever is nearby: "I feel really good right now, and I wanted you to know." Let the burst become a connection that will still be there tomorrow.

crash.text: Butler describes strong states as being carried beyond yourself — and knows that a return follows. It can be harsh: yesterday everything was shining, today it's grey and heavy. Butler reminds us that we are vulnerable and dependent beings: our state changes along with our body, our circumstances and other people. The comedown is neither payback for joy nor proof that something is wrong with you, but the ordinary rhythm of a being that doesn't live in an invulnerable fortress. Butler often speaks of a "livable life": not one where everything is good all the time, but one that can be borne. On days like these it is worth leaning on what makes life livable: sleep, food, the people close to you.
crash.practice: Wrap yourself in a blanket, make hot tea or cook something simple — and do it slowly, as a small ritual of care. A livable life is assembled from things like these.

panic.text: Butler thinks of a person as above all a body: openness to the world begins with a heart, a breath, skin, and the body can sense a threat before we understand anything. Right now, in a panic attack, your body knows this all too well: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, a sense that something terrible is about to happen sweeps over you. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Panic is an acute experience of the precariousness that Butler considers common to all people, not a sign of some special weakness of yours. Butler also stresses that vulnerability is also the capacity to respond, to feel support and being held. In a moment of panic you can look for the simplest support: the floor under your feet, your own exhale, an object in your hand.
panic.practice: Lean your back against a wall or press your feet into the floor — let yourself be held by what holds everyone. Make your exhale longer than your inhale and name aloud three supports your body is touching right now.

dread.text: Butler asks not "does life have meaning?" but "whose life will be mourned?" — and with that question turns the fear of finitude around. When the thought "what is all this for?" opens an abyss beneath your feet, the experience is very real. Butler speaks of precariousness: every life is fragile, and this is a condition shared by all living beings. But from this fragility Butler draws a conclusion not about meaninglessness but about connection: precisely because we are vulnerable, we need one another and can care for one another. The value of a life, for Butler, shows in its being "grievable" — that is, in how dear it is to someone and how much it is cherished. Existential dread touches on a truth — life is fragile — but not the whole truth. Fragility is also what connects you with others, and meaning lives precisely in these connections.
dread.practice: Go outside or to a window and find one living thing with your eyes — a bird, a tree, a passer-by. For a minute, look at it with the thought: this life is fragile too, and someone cherishes it.

fomo.text: A "frame," for Butler, is not just the edge of a photograph but whatever decides in advance which life will be visible and which will stay outside. The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are, once again, not there is exhausting and keeps you comparing endlessly. Extending Butler's thought, a social media feed is a frame too: it shows only selected scenes and quietly turns them into the norm. Your fear of missing out is a reaction not to other people's real lives but to a frame that makes some lives bright and others invisible. Your own ordinary life doesn't become any less real because of it. You can ask yourself who built the frame in which you suddenly find yourself "not there," and how — and what was left outside its edge.
fomo.practice: Put the phone down and look around: find one scene "outside the frame" — light on a wall, someone's hands, steam over a cup. Stay in it for a minute without showing it to anyone.

sleepless.text: At three in the morning, the precariousness Butler writes about stops being a concept and becomes the silence of the room. Thoughts grow louder and harsher, and morning seems endlessly far away. Butler reminds us that a person is not a self-sufficient fortress: we are vulnerable, and during the day we are held up by many invisible ties — conversations, tasks, the presence of others. At night these supports recede, and the precariousness shared by all people is felt more keenly. Night-time anxiety is not proof that everything really is bad, but a laid-bare experience of your own vulnerability in the silence. Butler sees vulnerability not as a verdict but as the ground of solidarity. And one more thing: at this very hour, others somewhere are also awake, with similar thoughts. You are not alone in this sleeplessness, even if it is dark and quiet around you.
sleepless.practice: Put one palm on your chest and the other on your belly, and feel your breath lifting and lowering you. In your mind, wish a good night to everyone behind the neighbouring windows who is also awake right now.

betrayal.text: Skin that feels a caress also feels a cut — Butler describes the human being in much this way: openness to care cannot be separated from openness to injury. Betrayal strikes precisely where you were open, and it truly hurts. In Precarious Life, Butler shows that vulnerability cannot be eliminated — we can only choose how to respond to it. After a betrayal you want to close yourself off forever, but the dream of total invulnerability, for Butler, leads to hardening rather than to safety. Your pain doesn't prove that trusting was foolish. You can allow yourself anger and grief, take time to recover, and still not give up the openness you are made of.
betrayal.practice: Wrap your arms around your shoulders and hold yourself like that for a minute: one arm for the anger and grief, the other for the openness you don't want to lose. You don't need to decide anything, just hold.

jealousy.text: One of Butler's best-known formulas: in love and desire we are "undone" by each other — the other becomes part of our "I," and the threat of losing them feels like a threat to ourselves. Hence the grip that takes hold of you completely: the fear of losing, the wish to hold on, shame at that wish. Jealousy is not an ugly weakness but a painful testimony to how connected you are with the other. But Butler also insists on the "opacity" of every person: the other can never be fully known, let alone be our property. That is exactly why an encounter with them is possible at all. You can acknowledge jealousy without turning it into control: ask yourself which part of your "I" feels threatened, and take care of that part first.
jealousy.practice: Picture the person you love at a moment when they are alone: looking out a window, thinking about something. Say to yourself: "You have a world I don't know" — and notice what rises: fear or tenderness.

resentment.text: Antigone buries her brother against the king's decree, and Butler devotes a book to her: what happens when someone's pain is refused recognition? An old grudge is like such an unburied story, carried for years because real pain lies behind it. Butler, continuing Hegel's line of thought, writes a lot about recognition: we vitally need to be seen and to have our pain acknowledged. Resentment often lasts so long because the harm was never acknowledged — neither by the one who caused it nor by those around. It keeps the truth about what happened when nobody else is keeping it. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler reflects on how to break cycles of retaliatory harm without denying the harm itself. You don't have to forgive or forget. You can acknowledge what happened yourself — give yourself the recognition others didn't give — and then the resentment may become a little lighter.
resentment.practice: Say aloud, slowly, the one sentence of acknowledgment you never received: "What happened to you was unjust." Say it the way a witness would.

heartbreak.text: In Precarious Life Butler writes about mourning as if describing the end of love: when the other leaves, we lose not only them but the part of ourselves that existed alongside them. A breakup can feel exactly like that — as if you had been taken apart. That is why after a breakup it is hard to understand who you are now. Butler doesn't suggest quickly "pulling yourself together": to grieve is to agree to a change whose outcome cannot be known in advance. And one more thing: loss, for Butler, not only isolates but also connects — almost everyone knows this pain, and in it you are not alone. A broken heart is not a defeat but a testimony to how deeply you are able to connect with others.
heartbreak.practice: Call a friend who has been through a breakup and ask: "How did you put yourself back together back then?" Listen to the answer — for Butler, loss not only divides but also connects.

quote.text: Loss has made a tenuous "we" of us all.
quote.author: Judith Butler

impostor.text: For Butler, "being yourself" is always a bit of a performance: even gender is not a hidden essence inside but something performed over and over. The fear of being found out any minute makes every success fragile, but this idea offers an unexpected comfort. Extending Butler's thought, a professional role works the same way: there is no "real" expert hidden somewhere deep inside, only repeated actions out of which the role is made. Then the feeling "I'm only pretending" doesn't expose you — it merely notices how all roles are made. Those who look confident are performing their roles too; they just doubt them less. Your performance is not a fake: skill and competence are also born of repetition. You are not deceiving others; you are taking part, like everyone else.
impostor.practice: Write down three things you have done in your role dozens of times — that is the role, assembled from repetitions. Next to them add: "Everyone once performed this for the first time."

self_hatred.text: Nietzsche describes conscience as a "turning": a person turns against themselves a force they could not direct outward — and Butler builds a book on that image. If your inner critic sounds so cruel that it seems like the truth, remember where that turn came from. In The Psychic Life of Power, drawing on Freud and Nietzsche, Butler describes how conscience forms when external demands and reproaches turn inward — and a person begins to treat themselves the way they were once treated. The critic is not your essence but an internalized voice of power that over time came to sound from within. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler adds that no one can know themselves fully, so ethics calls for leniency, including toward yourself. The critic's verdict is not the last word. You can listen to it without agreeing, and notice whose tone it speaks in.
self_hatred.practice: Say your inner critic's sentence out loud, then repeat it in a cartoon character's voice or very slowly. Notice how, stripped of its familiar tone of authority, the verdict loses weight.

quote.text: If we speak and try to give an account from this place, we will not be irresponsible, or, if we are, we will surely be forgiven.
quote.author: Judith Butler

helplessness.text: One person sitting down in a square is a gesture; when hundreds sit down beside them, it becomes an assembly, and Butler wrote a whole book about it. Feeling powerless to change anything is heavy, and it often rests on reality: some circumstances are stronger than any one person. Butler distinguishes between precariousness, shared by everyone, and precarity — the unequal distribution of vulnerability, in which some people are far less protected than others. Your helplessness may be not a personal weakness but an honest reaction to conditions that really do constrain you. But Butler doesn't stop there. In The Force of Nonviolence and other works, vulnerability is understood as what connects people: where no one can manage alone, people act together. One person's helplessness is not the same as the powerlessness of many. Even admitting "I can't do this alone" is already a step toward connection.
helplessness.practice: Go somewhere there are people — a courtyard, a café, a park — and simply spend a minute among other bodies that are carrying something too. One person's helplessness is not the helplessness of many.

procrastination.text: Picture an actor who won't go on stage for fear of performing imperfectly — for Butler, we all take part in such a show every day. "I can't get started" is a state in which it's easy to start gnawing at yourself. Butler's thinking can be applied like this: in every task we are not only acting but also performing a norm — of the "productive," "responsible" person — and this performance is expected to be flawless. Performativity, for Butler, is never perfect: we always repeat norms with deviations, glitches, hesitations. Putting things off is one such glitch: resistance to a demand that feels too heavy or alien. This doesn't make the task unnecessary, but it changes your view: you are not "broken"; you have run into a norm that presses on you. You can ask whose measure this is — and begin not with a perfect performance but with an imperfect one.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and do a "bad rehearsal" of the first step: a clumsy draft, a single line, a call without preparation. A rehearsal doesn't have to go well.

uprooted.text: We are called by name, in our native tongue, in a familiar tone — for Butler, that is how we become ourselves. Moving or emigrating takes away not only your home but this web of voices that knew you. Butler stresses that our "I" rests on recognition: we become ourselves in the eyes of others, in language, in familiar roles. In a new place this web is torn — nobody knows you, your language sounds foreign, your familiar ways of being yourself don't work. Butler also writes about "dispossession": we never fully belong to ourselves and always depend in part on others. This knowledge is bitter, but there is hope in it too: since the "I" is created in ties, it can grow again in new ones. Roots are not only the past left back there, but also the ties that are slowly being woven here.
uprooted.practice: Today, call one person in the new place by their name — a neighbour, a shop assistant, a colleague — and ask how they are. Recognition works both ways: the first thread can start with you.

overload.text: Butler asks us to remember, with every image, that someone chose what went into the frame. When news and feeds never end and your head feels about to burst, there are simply too many frames, each demanding a response. In Frames of War, Butler shows that everything we see has been selected and shaped in advance by frames: some lives and events end up at the centre, others outside the picture. A feed is an enormous machine of frames, and it demands that you respond to everything at once: grieve, be outraged, rejoice every few seconds. Your overload is not an inability to "take the hit" but the natural limit of a feeling being. Butler values an attentive, slow response to another. Stepping out of the stream doesn't mean becoming indifferent: sometimes it is the only way to truly notice even one person or one story.
overload.practice: Turn your phone face down and sit in silence for three minutes, looking at one still object in the room. When you want to check the feed, just notice the urge and return to the object.

unreality.text: Shout in the mountains and the echo returns your voice: Butler thinks the reality of the "I" rests on similar responses. If the world, or you yourself, feels unreal right now, that is very unsettling, and it deserves to be spoken of gently. Butler doesn't write about this experience directly, but would probably point out: the sense of reality is not born in solitude. We feel real when we are recognized — when someone responds, names us, knows us. For Butler, the "I" is not a closed fortress but an interweaving of relationships; when the threads loosen, or life passes under heavy strain, reality can lose its density. Unreality is not proof that you "aren't there," but a signal of a lack of response. Reality can come back through simple things: someone's voice, touching an object, your own name spoken aloud.
unreality.practice: Say your name out loud and hear how it sounds in the room. Then touch three surfaces — fabric, wood, water — and name each one: the world is answering.

awe.text: Butler reminds us that we breathe the same air as trees, the sea and strangers. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare moment when you feel this directly and seem to forget yourself. Butler describes strong states as "ecstatic" in the original sense of the word: we find ourselves "beside ourselves," taken beyond our own limits. Butler usually speaks of this in relation to grief or passion, but the same holds for awe. Awe is not a loss of self but a reminder that you have been open to the world and to others from the very beginning, that your "I" doesn't end at the boundary of your skin. This experience doesn't need to be analyzed or justified. You can simply let it last — and notice how, within it, the usual pressure to be separate and self-sufficient disappears.
awe.practice: Stay silent for two minutes beside whatever filled you with awe — no photos, no words. Take a few breaths and notice that this air is shared by you and everything around you.

relief.text: A bridge's supports only become noticeable once the load finally rolls off — Butler often reminds us that we too are held by invisible supports. Relief is that very moment: tension lets go, and your body exhales before you even realize it. Butler reminds us that we are vulnerable, bodily beings who are always bearing something: uncertainty, waiting, dependence on circumstances and on others. Relief makes visible how much strength went into that bearing. Butler would probably add that relief often comes not only from within but also thanks to others: someone helped, something was resolved, the world turned out to be a little kinder. So in relief there is also gratitude to the ties that hold us. There's no need to hastily devalue it with worry about the future. You can give yourself time to feel: things have become easier right now, and that is true.
relief.practice: Say thank you to whoever helped this relief come about — call, send a voice message or say it in person. If it was circumstances, simply breathe out aloud: "Thank you."

calm.text: If life is a series of roles, then calm, extending Butler's thought, is like the backstage: the make-up is still on, but no one is watching. It is a state in which you need neither to defend nor to prove anything. Butler writes a lot about how norms demand constant performance from us: to be the "right" kind of worker, partner, person. These demands sound almost all the time, even when we don't notice them. Calm is a rare pause in this endless performance: a moment when no role requires confirmation. For Butler, a "livable life" is a life in which you can breathe without being under constant threat. Your calm is a small embodiment of such a life. It doesn't need to be justified by productivity or earned. You can notice it and let it be — even for a few minutes.
calm.practice: Sit down and let your face go "off duty": relax your forehead, your jaw, the corners of your mouth. Stay for a minute without any expression meant for anyone.

inspiration.text: A word said for the first time differently from how it has always been said is a small rebellion, and Butler builds a whole philosophy on such rebellions. Inspiration feels similar: a new possibility has opened, and you want to bring it to life. Butler gives possibility enormous importance: for people hemmed in by norms, the mere appearance of another way to live, speak or be can change everything. Performativity, for Butler, means that we are not doomed to repeat the same thing: every repetition holds a chance of a shift. Inspiration is the experience of such a shift from within, the moment when you see that things can be otherwise. Butler also reminds us that we never create alone: language, images and other people's voices pass through us. You can cherish inspiration as a gift that came from your connections — and not demand immediate perfection from it.
inspiration.practice: Write down in one sentence the possibility that has opened, and beneath it a voice — a book, a person, a song — that helped it appear. Don't plan, just record it.

quote.text: Possibility is not a luxury; it is as crucial as bread.
quote.author: Judith Butler

schadenfreude.text: Anyone can make a mistake, lose, stumble — Butler calls this precariousness and considers it shared by all. Almost nobody admits to secret joy at someone else's failure, though probably everyone has felt it — and it is directly tied to that knowledge. Living with this knowledge is hard, and, in Butler's view, people and whole societies often try to push vulnerability outward — to attribute it to "others" so as to feel invulnerable themselves. Schadenfreude is a brief breather: the failure happened to someone else, not to me. This is not a verdict on your character; rather, it is a sign of how hard it is to carry your own fragility. If you acknowledge that everyone is vulnerable, someone else's failure can turn from relief into recognition.
schadenfreude.practice: Picture the person whose failure pleased you on the evening of that same day — at home, alone with it. Which of your own fears is reflected in that picture? Name it to yourself.

contempt.text: The English word "matter" means both material and significance, and Butler turns this pun into the question of Bodies That Matter (1993): how does society decide whose lives and bodies "matter" and whose don't? Contempt, so hard to admit, often hides hurt, tiredness or fear underneath — and it is tied to this sorting. The sorting itself, for Butler, is not natural: it is created by norms that we all absorb, often without noticing. Contempt is a moment when this sorting kicks in within us and someone ends up "lower." The feeling itself is not a verdict on you, but it is worth questioning. Whose norm is it protecting? And what about this person stings you so much that you want to put them beyond the line? Sometimes behind contempt lies your own pain that was never given room.
contempt.practice: Imagine this person is the main character of a film, and you watch one scene of their day through their eyes. What can you see in it that makes them "matter" too?

disgust.text: Peel, mould, a stranger's hair in your plate — Julia Kristeva calls "abject" whatever we push away in order to draw the boundaries of our own self, and Butler takes up the concept. Disgust is a strong bodily "no" to such things: to a person, a situation, sometimes to your own body or actions; it arises quickly and seems natural. For Butler, these boundaries are not given by nature; they are maintained by constant rejection — and are therefore always a little shaky. Disgust is the work of a boundary: this is how the psyche protects what it takes to be itself. This is useful to know about self-disgust too: sometimes we push away in ourselves what others once called "unacceptable." Disgust doesn't need to be suppressed. But you can ask: which boundary is it guarding right now — and do I need that boundary in this form?
disgust.practice: When disgust rolls in, breathe out slowly and rest a palm gently on your solar plexus. Say to yourself: "A boundary runs here — is it mine?" — and wait for your body to loosen a little.

revenge.text: "An eye for an eye" looks like fair accounting, but Butler notices that such accounts never close. You were hurt, and everything in you demands an answer. In Precarious Life, written after September 11, 2001, Butler reflects on how quickly grief and pain turn into a thirst for retribution — in individuals and in whole societies. Butler doesn't deny anger, but suggests staying with the grief itself and not rushing to "resolve" it with a retaliatory blow. Revenge promises to restore the lost control, as if you could become invulnerable again. But for Butler, a wound reveals the truth of shared vulnerability, and a wound in return doesn't cancel it. Your desire for revenge is a signal of how deep the pain is and of an injustice that needs to be named. It can be given a voice — in words, in a demand for justice — without causing harm.
revenge.practice: Before you think about a response, give yourself five minutes of grief: sit down, put a hand on the place in your body where it hurts, and stay silently with what was taken from you.

anger_at_loved.text: Melanie Klein watched an infant both love and bite the same breast: love and aggression are intertwined from the very beginning, because we depend most on those we love. Butler takes up this idea in The Force of Nonviolence (2020) — and it helps with one of the most shameful and most ordinary feelings, anger at a partner, parents, children. Dependence gives birth to both tenderness and rage. Butler draws an important conclusion from this: nonviolence is not the absence of aggression but a practice of dealing with it, the skill of holding it so that it doesn't destroy the bond. Your anger doesn't cancel your love and doesn't make you a bad parent or partner. It says that you feel cramped, burdened, or that something is missing. You can acknowledge it — and express it in words, not in an action that wounds.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger rises, step into another room or onto the balcony for a minute and take five slow breaths out. Say to yourself: "I'm angry, and I love" — and go back when your voice has quieted.

ambivalence.text: A child cannot help loving those who care for it, even when that care is hard — in The Psychic Life of Power Butler calls this "passionate attachment," inevitably double-edged. Loving a person and at the same time not being able to stand them is hard, but a very common combination. Out of these early ties grows the adult mixture of tenderness and protest, gratitude and the wish to pull away. Your ambivalence is not a sign that something is wrong with love, but an honest trace of the dependence we are all made of. You don't have to choose one feeling and renounce the other. You can let them sit side by side and see what each is saying.
ambivalence.practice: Hold both palms out in front of you: in one, place in your mind what you love this person for; in the other, what is hard with them. Hold them like that for a minute without comparing which is heavier.

guilty_relief.text: For Butler, grief is weather, not a plan: it brings whatever feelings it brings. Relief after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a gravely ill loved one often comes together with shame: how can you feel lightness if you love them? Butler writes about grief as a state that resists full control and clarity. Following Freud, Butler notes that when we lose a person, we don't always know what exactly we have lost along with them — loss is enigmatic even to ourselves. Much can come together in it: love, tiredness, release from long tension, mourning for the life that existed before the illness or the discord. Relief is not betrayal but one of the threads in the complex fabric of grief. Grief changes us unpredictably, and there is no "correct" set of feelings you are supposed to have. Love and relief can exist together.
guilty_relief.practice: Walk slowly around the room or down the street and with each step silently name one feeling: love, relief, sadness, tiredness… Let them walk side by side, without taking turns.

indifference.text: Some deaths reach the front page with names and faces, others as a line of numbers, and Butler asks who decides what moves us. If someone's grief or a major event leaves you quiet inside, and that frightens you, this question matters. In Frames of War, Butler shows that our feelings are never born in a vacuum: what moves us is largely determined by "frames" — the ways stories and images are presented, selected and repeated. Butler writes that our very affects are regulated: some losses are framed so as to evoke mourning, others so that they pass us by. Your indifference is not proof of heartlessness but, perhaps, the trace of a frame, or tiredness from the constant stream. Butler adds that frames are not airtight: they have cracks through which feeling unexpectedly breaks through. You can wait for such a moment without demanding it of yourself.
indifference.practice: Find the story of one particular person connected to the event — a name, a face, a few lines about their life — and read it slowly, once. Don't demand a feeling from yourself; just give it a chance.

escape.text: A suit that once fit starts to pinch — that is roughly how Butler describes the norms we live by. The urge to drop everything — job, city, role — can be very strong. This is not about leaving life, but about wanting to live differently. One of Butler's main questions is: what makes a life "livable"? In Undoing Gender, Butler writes that such norms can both sustain us and squeeze us unbearably. A role — the good employee, the model parent, the reliable person — also rests on repetition. And since it is repeated, it can be repeated a little differently: that is performativity as Butler understands it. The wish to escape is a signal that some norm has become too tight, not a whim. You don't have to tear everything down at once. You can find where, in the daily "performance" of your role, you could make a small shift.
escape.practice: Today, do one thing in your role "off script": a different route to work, a different greeting, lunch on a bench instead of at your desk. Notice how much freedom fits into a small shift.

forbidden_attraction.text: In Butler's first book, Subjects of Desire (1987), desire is not "I want" but a road: the "I" goes out of itself to find itself in another. Attraction to someone unavailable or "wrong" often comes unbidden and unsettles you, and Butler passes no moral verdict on it — neither will we. Later, Butler shows that society marks out in advance which desires count as "intelligible" and acceptable. An attraction that is "not allowed" is not evidence of corruption but a sign that desire is always wider than the frames assigned to it. Deciding what to do with it is not the task of this minute. You can simply ask: what in me is this desire reaching for — what freedom, aliveness, new self?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Close your eyes and imagine who you become near this person: how your voice sounds, how you move. Pick one such quality and think where else in your present life you could allow it.

social_anxiety.text: Butler recalls Althusser's scene: a policeman shouts "Hey, you!" and a person turns around, becoming the one addressed. Fear of others' judgment, when your body tenses and words stick, is a sensitivity to such a call. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler writes that we become ourselves by being "addressed": others speak to us, name us, wait for a reply — long before we have chosen anything. That is why judgment stings so much: it touches the very foundation of the "I." But Butler adds something important: no one is fully transparent to themselves, and no one can present themselves flawlessly. This is a shared condition, not your personal shortcoming. Awkwardness among people is not a failure but an honest expression of the opacity everyone has. Others are most likely more preoccupied with their own anxiety than with yours.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, silently greet each person you see before they look at you: "Hi, you're nervous about something too." To call out first is to be a little less the one who is called.

uncertainty.text: Tomorrow belongs to no one — not to you, your bosses or governments — and Butler makes this not a reason for fear but the starting point of ethics. Uncertainty is exhausting: it's unclear what will happen, and there is nothing to lean on. Butler suggests seeing it not as a malfunction but as a shared condition of life. We depend on others, on circumstances, on the world — this is precariousness. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler writes that ethics asks us to risk ourselves precisely in moments of unknowingness, when what formed us diverges from what lies before us. Not knowing, for Butler, is not only a threat but also a place where change and a new connection with others become possible. Uncertainty doesn't have to be "defeated"; it can be borne — and better together. You don't need to know everything in advance to take the next step.
uncertainty.practice: Tell someone close, out loud: "I don't know what will happen with…" — and ask what they don't know. Shared not-knowing weighs less.

waiting.text: A doctor, a committee, a postman — Butler reminds us that our life is always partly in other hands, and this is a shared condition, not personal helplessness. Waiting for an answer, results or news is hard precisely because so little depends on you right now. In Frames of War, Butler writes that precariousness means living among others: our fate depends on the decisions, care and actions of people we sometimes don't even know. Waiting lays this dependence bare especially sharply. But Butler doesn't consider it humiliating: it is the ground of solidarity, since others depend on us in just the same way. Your restlessness is an honest reaction to the fact that you don't control everything. While the waiting lasts, you can turn your attention to the part of life that really is in your hands right now — and to those who are waiting beside you.
waiting.practice: While you wait, do one thing with your hands that is definitely in your power: wash a cup, water a plant, make the bed. Do it slowly, feeling: this part is mine.

quote.text: Precariousness implies living socially, that is, the fact that one's life is always in some sense in the hands of the other.
quote.author: Judith Butler

regret.text: Butler calls the demand to be fully transparent and consistent "ethical violence" — even when it's your own. Regret over something said, done or left undone keeps coming back, often in exactly that voice. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler shows that we can never give a full account of ourselves: much in us was formed before we could choose, by other people and by circumstances, and we are not transparent even to ourselves. Yet when we look back, we judge our past selves as if we had known then everything we know now. Butler doesn't remove responsibility but understands it differently — not as a demand for flawlessness, but as a readiness to answer to others while acknowledging our own limits. Your regret shows that you care, and that is valuable. A simple thought can soften it: back then, you acted with the knowledge and the strength you had.
regret.practice: Picture yourself at the moment you regret and say one sentence to that person out loud: "Back then you didn't know…" Say it in the tone a kind friend would use.

longing.text: "Who are you?" — the Italian philosopher Adriana Cavarero considers this question more important than "what are you?", and Butler places it at the heart of Giving an Account of Oneself. When you miss a particular person, the pain has a name and a face — it answers exactly that "who." Each person is unique, and their story truly comes together only when someone else sees it and can tell it. A person close to you is someone who knows your story and holds on to it. That is why longing runs so deep: you miss not only their presence but also the one who saw you in exactly that way. Your longing is not weakness but a recognition of their uniqueness and of your bond. It doesn't need to be "let go" on command. You can let it live in memory and in the stories you tell about them.
longing.practice: Tell someone — a friend, a relative, or simply an empty room out loud — one short story about how this person was when they were with you. For Cavarero and Butler, a story lives as long as it is told.

world_pain.text: In the squares of many cities people light candles for strangers — for Butler, that is precisely the recognition that another's life was precious. Pain for those suffering from war, disaster, injustice can be almost unbearable, especially when the news comes in a continuous stream. In Frames of War, Butler asks: which lives do we recognize as "grievable," that is, worthy of being mourned? And answers: every life deserves mourning — regardless of country, language or side. Your pain is neither weakness nor "excessive sensitivity," but the capacity to recognize the value of the lives of people you have never seen. Butler doesn't suggest carrying it all alone: mourning, for Butler, connects people and can become the ground of solidarity. You can allow yourself to grieve — and look for those with whom this pain can be shared.
world_pain.practice: Switch off the screen and stand at a window for a minute, silently thinking of those who are suffering — without choosing who deserves that minute. Then talk with someone who also cares.

rejection.text: A thirty-second casting call is a good picture of recognition for Butler: they see not all of you, only how well you fit the role. Rejection hurts because it touches the deep need to be recognized. Butler shows that this need is not a whim: we exist as social beings only insofar as someone recognizes us. Yet the conditions of recognition are not set by us, nor by any one person. In Undoing Gender, Butler writes that these conditions are created by society and change over time — they shape ideas about who "fits," who is good, attractive or successful "enough." When you are rejected, it is often just such a norm at work, not some deep knowledge of you. Rejection is an event within particular frames, not a final verdict on your worth. The pain of it is real. But it doesn't have the last word on who you are.
rejection.practice: Write down the "norm" you may have been judged by — in one line, like a casting notice. Below it, list three qualities of yours that the notice doesn't mention.

abandonment.text: An infant doesn't choose the arms that hold it and cannot survive without them — Butler considers this original dependence not a childhood remnant to be outgrown but a permanent feature of human life. That is why the fear of being abandoned has such deep roots and feels so sharp. In Precarious Life, Butler writes that from the very beginning we are given over to others — before we are able to choose anything. That is why the threat of losing someone close resonates so deeply: it touches the very foundation. Your fear is not "excessive attachment" but the memory of a fundamental vulnerability shared by everyone. Butler suggests not being ashamed of dependence but widening its circle: we are held not by one person but by many ties — friendship, communities, mutual care. These can be noticed and strengthened.
abandonment.practice: Today, send a few warm words to one person in your circle — not the one you're afraid of losing, but a friend, a neighbour, a community. That is how the circle that holds you widens.

unrequited.text: Love, for Butler, is not a bargain but a carrying beyond yourself — it need not come back in kind. Without an answer, it hurts in a particular way. Butler writes that in love and desire we find ourselves "beside ourselves" — we are carried toward the other and are no longer quite the masters of our feelings. This is not a sign of weakness but a property of any passionate bond. When there is no answer, this openness is left without support, and it seems you gave yourself in vain. But there is another way to see it: the capacity to go beyond yourself like this is valuable and not so common, and it doesn't vanish because this time it met no answer. Your love has already changed you. In time, this openness will find somewhere to flow.
unrequited.practice: Put a palm on your chest and silently list three things you saw or felt thanks to this love. Tell yourself: "This stays with me."

humiliation.text: In 2017 protesters in São Paulo burned an effigy of Butler labelled "witch"; Butler replied with a calm essay on why gender frightens people. Humiliation burns because it strikes at your dignity, in front of others — Butler knows this not only from books. In Excitable Speech (1997), Butler explores how words wound: an insult, a nickname, mockery act almost like a blow. Butler explains this by the fact that we exist in language — we are called, named, and through this we become ourselves. That is why a wounding word strikes deep. But Butler also offers hope: the speaker doesn't fully own their words; their meaning can be contested, rethought, turned around. Many hurtful names have since been reclaimed by those they were meant to wound. Humiliation speaks of the one who humiliated you, not of who you are — and the last word about you is not theirs.
humiliation.practice: Say the wounding word out loud in your own voice — slowly, calmly, like a stranger's object you are examining in your palm. Then add one sentence of your own in reply.

body_shame.text: A mirror, for Butler, is not neutral glass: in it we see other people's gazes that moved into us long ago. If you're unhappy with your body right now, it's not your fault. In Gender Trouble, Butler shows that much of what seems "natural" about the body and how it ought to be is created by norms repeated again and again until they look like nature. But what is created by repetition is not final: it can be repeated differently. In Precarious Life, Butler adds that the body never belongs only to us: from the very beginning it is open to the gaze, touch and care of others — and so it is sensitive to others' judgment. Your dissatisfaction is largely the voice of internalized norms, not the truth about you. You can notice your body not only as something judged but as what you live and feel through.
body_shame.practice: For a minute, with your eyes closed, feel your body from the inside — the warmth of your palms, the weight of your legs, the movement of your breath — without looking at it from outside. Name one sensation your body gave you today.

illness.text: A hospital ward reveals what health hides: other people feed us, wash us, lift us — and Butler considers this picture the truth about everyone, not an exception. When your body lets you down, the familiar feeling that you can rely on yourself collapses. It is frightening and infuriating, and these feelings are legitimate. Butler suggests seeing the body's vulnerability not as a defeat but as a shared condition of life. We were never fully independent: from birth we need care, food, shelter, other people. Illness merely makes this dependence visible. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler writes about interdependence as what binds all living beings, not only "the weak." Needing help is nothing to be ashamed of: it is not a deviation from the norm of human life but its essence, which health temporarily hides. You can allow yourself to accept care without apologizing for it.
illness.practice: Today, ask for one kind of help — briefly, without apologies or explanations: "Could you please…?" Notice that asking is part of shared life, not a debt.

pride.text: No one builds a house alone, even if only one name is on the plaque — Butler reminds us that every action rests on others. Pride in what you have done is a good feeling, and you don't have to hide it behind modesty. Butler helps you see two sides to it. The first is action: for Butler, we are not simply "the way we are"; we become ourselves through what we do and repeat. What you have seen through is part of who you are becoming. The second side is connection: in Notes Toward a Performative Theory of Assembly (2015), Butler stresses that no one acts alone, and our ability to do anything rests on the support of others, on language, on infrastructure. Healthy pride doesn't contradict gratitude but complements it. You can take pleasure in your contribution — and notice those who made it possible. One doesn't diminish the other.
pride.practice: Say out loud what you're proud of — in a full sentence, without "oh, it's nothing." Then, in your mind or in person, thank one person without whom it wouldn't have happened.

melancholy.text: In The Psychic Life of Power Butler takes up a remarkable formula from Freud: character is "a precipitate of abandoned attachments"; losses don't disappear but become us. Butler develops the thought: we carry those we loved within us — in gestures, pet words, intonations, often without noticing. Bright sadness, where grief sits alongside tenderness, sounds like the voice of that precipitate — it needs neither to be chased away nor cured. Melancholy is a moment when these inner traces become audible: the past sounds in the present. This is not a breakdown or being stuck, but the memory of a love that goes on living in you. You can accept bright sadness as a quiet acknowledgment of what shaped you.
melancholy.practice: Find in yourself one habit, word or gesture inherited from someone or something you lost — and repeat it now on purpose, with tenderness. Let it be a small bow to the past.
